title: Unit 4c - Vectors Introduction
summary: Title slide introducing the Vectors unit in CS 103, covering the C++ vector container class. Presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 4c on Vectors in the CS 103 course. The unit covers the C++ vector class, which is a key data structure in the Standard Template Library (STL). Vectors provide a managed, resizable array implementation that is widely used in C++ programming. This unit will cover how vectors work, their member functions, performance characteristics, and practical usage tips.
notes_text: Vectors are one of the most commonly used containers in C++ and understanding them is essential for effective C++ programming.

title: Vector Class Overview
summary: Introduces the vector class as a full-featured managed array that grows automatically, performs deep copies, tracks size, and supports random access indexing.
main_text: The vector class is a full-featured, managed array implementation with several key capabilities. It will grow the array as needed, meaning you do not have to worry about running out of space. It will perform deep copies, so assigning one vector to another creates an independent copy of all elements. It tracks its size automatically, so you always know how many elements are stored. It still allows array-like indexing (also known as random-access) such as data[i], making it familiar to use. It also provides several other capabilities beyond basic arrays. The vector class is similar to Java's ArrayList or Python's list objects, providing dynamic array functionality. More details can be found in the online documentation for the C++ standard library.
notes_text: The vector class solves the key limitations of raw C++ arrays: fixed size, no built-in size tracking, and shallow copy behavior. Understanding these advantages helps explain why vectors are preferred over raw arrays in most C++ code.

title: C++ Standard Template Library (STL)
summary: Introduces the C++ STL as a collection of templatized container classes including vector, list, deque, set, priority_queue, and map.
main_text: C++ has defined a whole set of templatized classes for you to use out of the box, known as the Standard Template Library (STL). The STL includes several important container classes: vector<T> for dynamic arrays, list<T> for linked lists, deque<T> for double-ended queues, set<T> for ordered unique collections, priority_queue<T> for heap-based priority queues, and map<K,V> for key-value associative containers. The T in angle brackets represents a template parameter that specifies the type of data the container will hold. These containers and their implementation are the focus of CS 104, the follow-up course. In CS 103, the focus is on learning how to use these containers, particularly vectors.
notes_text: The STL is a fundamental part of modern C++ programming. Each container has different performance characteristics suited for different use cases. Vectors are covered here, while the full details of all these containers are explored in CS 104.

title: Templates and C++ STL Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide transitioning to the topic of Templates and the C++ Standard Template Library.
main_text: This is a section divider slide marking the transition to the topic of Templates and the C++ Standard Template Library. Templates are the mechanism that allows STL containers like vector to work with any data type. Understanding templates is important for understanding how containers in the STL are designed and used.
notes_text: Templates are a core C++ feature that enables generic programming, allowing code to be written once and used with many different types.

title: Templates - The Problem of Code Duplication
summary: Motivates C++ templates by showing the problem of duplicating linked list code for different data types like int and double.
main_text: Previously, a linked list was built to store integers. But what if we want a list of doubles or chars or other objects? Without templates, we would have to define the same code but with different types, which is wasteful duplication. For example, an IntItem struct contains an int val and IntItem* next pointer, and its ListInt class has push_back(int newval). Similarly, a DoubleItem struct contains a double val and DoubleItem* next pointer, and its ListDouble class has push_back(double newval). The code is essentially identical except for the types used. Enter C++ Templates, which allow one set of code to work for any type the programmer wants, eliminating this code duplication problem.
notes_text: This slide motivates why templates exist. Without them, every new data type would require writing a separate version of the same data structure, leading to maintenance nightmares and code bloat. Templates solve this by parameterizing the type.

images.description: Two code blocks showing duplicate struct and class definitions: IntItem/ListInt for integers and DoubleItem/ListDouble for doubles, illustrating the code duplication problem that templates solve.

title: Templates - Declaring and Using Templatized Code
summary: Shows how C++ templates allow type parameterization so one class definition works for int, double, or any custom type like Quad.
main_text: C++ Templates allow the type of variable to be a parameter (variable) specified by the programmer. The compiler will generate separate class/struct code versions for any type desired when instantiated as an object. To declare templatized code, use the syntax 'template <typename T>' before the struct or class definition. For example, a generic Item struct uses 'T val' and 'Item<T>* next', and a generic List class uses 'void push_back(T newval)' with 'Item<T>* head' as a private member. To use templatized code, specify the type in angle brackets when creating objects: List<int> ilist causes an int version of the code to be generated by the compiler, List<double> dlist causes a double version, and List<Quad> qlist causes a Quad version. Usage is then straightforward: ilist.push_back(5), dlist.push_back(5.5125), double x = dlist.pop_front(), int y = ilist.pop_front().
notes_text: The 'template <typename T>' syntax tells the compiler that T is a placeholder for a real type. The compiler generates concrete code for each type used, a process called template instantiation. This is a compile-time mechanism with no runtime overhead.

images.description: Code block showing template declaration with 'template <typename T>' for a generic Item struct and List class, followed by usage in main() creating List<int> and List<double> objects with push_back and pop_front operations.

title: Vector Class Usage and Operations
summary: Demonstrates vector as a resizable container with code showing initialization, push_back, indexing, front/back access, erase, and insert operations.
main_text: The vector is a container class where what it contains is determined by the programmer via a template. It implements an array-based list that can be used like (and gives the benefits of) an array but can resize automatically. A complete code example demonstrates key operations: (0) vector<int> my_vec(5) creates a vector with initial size of 5. (1) Elements can be set using array-style indexing: my_vec[i] = i+50 fills with values 50-54. (1) push_back adds elements to the end: my_vec.push_back(10) and my_vec.push_back(8) append values. (2) Elements can be modified by index: my_vec[0] = 30. Iteration uses my_vec.size() to get the count and my_vec[i] to access elements. (3) back() and front() return the last and first elements respectively. pop_back() removes the last element. (4) erase(my_vec.begin() + 2) removes the element at index 2. insert(my_vec.begin() + 1, 43) inserts 43 at index 1. The diagrams show the array state after each operation, demonstrating how the vector contents change.
notes_text: The numbered steps trace through the code showing the vector state at each point. Notice how push_back grows the vector, erase shifts elements left to fill the gap, and insert shifts elements right to make room. The begin() function returns an iterator to the first element, and adding an offset gives access to other positions.

images.description: Five sequential diagrams showing the vector my_vec state at each step: (0) empty with unknown values, (1) filled with 50-54, (2) after push_back and modification showing [30,51,52,53,54,10,8], (3) after pop_back showing [30,51,52,53,54,10], (4) after erase and insert showing [30,43,51,53,54,10].

title: What Happens Behind the Scenes
summary: Explains vector internals: vectors store a pointer to a dynamically allocated array, track capacity and size, perform deep copies, and resize when needed.
main_text: Vectors abstract arrays. Behind the scenes, vectors are just creating and manipulating arrays but giving you a simplified set of operators and functions. Vectors store a pointer to the array (which must be dynamically allocated since it is of variable size), the capacity of the array, and the size of used/occupied elements. For example, a vector v1 created with initial size 5 and filled with values 50-54 has data pointer, cap=5, and size=5. When push_back(10) is called, the vector must resize because the array is full. It allocates a new larger array (capacity doubles to 10), copies the old elements over, adds the new element, and updates cap=10, size=6. A shallow copy would have both v1 and v2 pointing to the same underlying array, which is dangerous. Instead, vector assignment (v2 = v1) causes a deep copy where v2 gets its own separate copy of the entire array with its own data pointer, cap, and size values. When the destructor is called on v2 and v1, each safely deallocates its own array.
notes_text: Understanding the internal representation of vectors (data pointer, capacity, size) is crucial for understanding their performance. The capacity is often larger than the size to allow push_back to be fast most of the time. Deep copy on assignment prevents the dangling pointer problem that would occur with shallow copies.

images.description: Diagram showing vector v1 and v2 internal structure with data pointer, cap, and size fields. Shows the resize process when push_back overflows, and contrasts shallow copy (both pointing to same array, marked with prohibition sign) versus deep copy (v2 gets its own array). Arrows show pointer relationships.

title: Vector Class Member Functions Reference
summary: Comprehensive reference of vector member functions including constructor, operator[], push_back, pop_back, size, empty, front, back, erase, and insert.
main_text: The vector class provides the following member functions: The constructor can take an initial number of items or be left blank to create an empty vector. operator[] allows array-style indexed access such as myvec[i]. push_back(T new_val) adds a copy of new_val to the end of the array, allocating more memory if necessary. pop_back() removes the item at the back of the vector but does not return it. size() returns the current number of items stored as an unsigned int. empty() returns true if no items are in the vector. front() and back() return the item at the front or back respectively. erase(index) removes the item at the specified index, where the index is specified using begin() plus an offset. insert(index, T new_val) adds new_val at the specified index, also using begin() plus an offset. The accompanying code example demonstrates all of these operations in a complete program.
notes_text: Note that pop_back does not return the removed value, unlike pop operations in some other languages. To get the last value before removing it, call back() first, then pop_back(). The erase and insert functions use iterator-style indexing with begin() + offset rather than plain integer indices.

title: Understanding Vector Performance
summary: Analyzes vector performance trade-offs: O(1) random access and fast back operations are strengths, while front/middle insert/delete and resizing are weaknesses.
main_text: Vectors are good at some things and worse at others in terms of performance. The Good: Fast access for random access (accessing any index i is O(1) constant time). Allows for fast addition or removal of items at the back of the vector. The Bad: Inserting or removing an item at the front or in the middle requires shifting all items up or down to add or remove the item, making these operations O(n). Adding an item when the underlying array is full will trigger an O(n) resize operation where the vector will allocate a whole new block of memory and copy over every item. However, if implemented wisely, resize is not as bad as it sounds (more details in CS 104). The diagrams illustrate: when deleting from the middle (index 2), elements at indices 3-5 must shift left to fill the gap. When inserting beyond capacity, a completely new larger array must be allocated and all elements copied to the new location, with the new elements appended.
notes_text: The amortized cost of push_back is actually O(1) because resize operations happen increasingly rarely as the vector grows (capacity typically doubles). This amortized analysis is covered in CS 104. The key takeaway is: use vectors when you need fast random access and primarily add/remove from the back.

images.description: Two diagrams showing vector performance issues. Left diagram shows deleting element at index 2 from array [30,51,52,53,54,10] requiring elements to shift left, resulting in [30,51,53,54,10]. Right diagram shows array [30,51,53,54,10] needing to grow when adding 12 and 18, requiring allocation of a new larger array and copying all elements.

title: Vector Tips and Odds and Ends
summary: Covers important vector usage tips: use push_back for empty vectors, use unsigned int or size_t for loop indices, and vectors make copies when adding items.
main_text: Important: If you don't provide an initial size to the vector, you must add items using push_back(). Creating an empty vector with vector<int> myvec gives cap=0, size=0, and data pointer=0. Attempting to use myvec[i] = i+50 on an empty vector would cause a segfault because no memory has been allocated. Instead, use myvec.push_back(i+50) to add elements. When iterating over the items with a for loop, use 'unsigned int' or 'size_t' type to match the return type of size(). The correct loop syntax is: for(size_t i=0; i < myvec.size(); i++). When adding an item, a copy will be made to add to the vector. For example, with vector<string> v1 and string s1="abc", calling v1.push_back(s1) copies the string into the vector. If s1 is later changed to "xyz", v1[0] still prints "abc" because the vector stored an independent copy.
notes_text: The segfault when indexing an empty vector is a very common beginner mistake. The size() function returns size_t (unsigned integer type), so comparing with a signed int can cause compiler warnings or unexpected behavior with negative values. The copy semantics mean vectors are safe but may be slow for large objects.

images.description: Diagrams showing: an empty vector with cap=0, size=0, data=0; a populated vector with cap=5, size=5 pointing to array [50,51,52,53,54]; and a string vector showing s1 containing 'abc' being pushed into v1, where v1 stores its own copy so changing s1 to 'xyz' does not affect v1[0].

title: Vector Pass-By-Value
summary: Demonstrates that passing a vector by value to a function creates a deep copy, so modifications inside the function do not affect the original vector.
main_text: When passing a vector by value to a function, a deep copy is made. In the example, myvec is a vector<int> filled with values 50-54 using push_back (cap=5, size=5, data pointer at address 240). When do_it(myvec) is called, the function void do_it(vector<int> v) receives a complete deep copy of myvec. Inside do_it, v has its own separate data pointer (at address 760), cap=10, size=6 after v.push_back(60) adds 60 to the copy. The push_back(60) only adds to v (the copy), not to myvec. After do_it returns, iterating over myvec shows it is unchanged with its original 5 elements: 50, 51, 52, 53, 54. This is consistent with how other types work with pass-by-value in C++, but can be surprising and expensive for large vectors since every element must be copied.
notes_text: To avoid the cost of deep copying, pass vectors by reference (vector<int>& v) when you want to modify the original, or by const reference (const vector<int>& v) when you only need to read it. Pass-by-value copies can be very expensive for large vectors.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing myvec with data pointer at 240, cap=5, size=5 pointing to array [50,51,52,53,54], and the copy v inside do_it with data pointer at 760, cap=10, size=6 pointing to array [50,51,52,53,54,60,?,?,?,?]. Demonstrates that modifications to v do not affect myvec.

summary: Closing slide directing students to practice with in-class exercises on vectors.
main_text: This slide directs students to complete in-class exercises to practice using vectors. The exercises reinforce the concepts covered in this unit including vector creation, using push_back, pop_back, front, back, erase, insert, and understanding performance characteristics of vector operations.
notes_text: Hands-on practice is essential for mastering vector operations. Students should practice creating vectors, adding and removing elements, and understanding when different operations are efficient or inefficient.
